title: With Due Respect (Vol. 5) -- Ch. 6: Party-list Imponderables
primary_topics: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5) -- CJP's April 26, 2009 Inquirer column critiquing Banat v. Comelec, which raised party-list seats from 22 to 55 (ballooning the House toward 271) by upholding the 2-percent threshold's 'first clause' but striking down its 'second clause' as unconstitutional

His objection that the ruling produced 'preposterous' results -- awarding seats to parties with under 2 percent while capping topnotchers at three (Buhay's 7.33 percent got three seats, Cocofed's 0.98 percent got one) -- when the Court, bent on filling 55 seats, should have struck down both the three-seat limit and the 2-percent threshold (as Justice Nachura urged) for 'legal, mathematical, and proportional precision'

The 'doctrinal contradiction' he flags: the Court called the 20-percent allocation 'merely a ceiling,' yet under Banat reaching that ceiling became 'mandatory,' and the Court 'quietly overlooked' its own recent decisions unanimously reaffirming the Veterans formula -- even its ponentes concurring 'with nary a mention' ('So much for doctrinal stability and depth of conviction!')

His further problems and prescription: by inflating party-list seats the Court arguably pushed the House past the constitutional 250-member cap (did it 'usurp the law-making function'?), raising unanswered questions about salaries and the three-fourths Charter-change vote -- so 'Congress should take the initiative in correcting the deficiencies,' as the Court itself once urged
sub_topics: What Banat did: on April 21, 2009 the Court promulgated Banat v. Comelec, 'increasing the seats for party-list representatives from 22 to 55' and thereby enlarging the House toward 271

The threshold split: the Court upheld the 'first clause' of Section 1(b) of RA 7941, granting an initial seat to a party-list with 'at least two percent of the total votes cast,' but struck down as unconstitutional the 'second clause' (additional seats 'in proportion to their total number of votes') because it 'makes it mathematically impossible to achieve the maximum number of available party-list seats when the number... exceeds 50'

The 'preposterous' results: to fill the additional seats, the Court awarded slots to parties with under 2 percent while still capping topnotchers at three -- so Buhay Party (1,169,243 votes, 7.33 percent) got only three seats while Cocofed (155,920 votes, 0.98 percent) got one, and 'a party that gets only 1,000 votes can win. Preposterous, but certainly possible!'

CJP's alternative: 'since filling up 55 seats was its passion,' the Court should have declared unconstitutional 'both the three-seat limit and the 2-percent threshold' (the latter entirely, as Justice Nachura's separate opinion did) so it could compute allocations 'with legal, mathematical, and proportional precision' and avoid the absurd scenarios

The doctrinal contradiction: the Court ruled the 20-percent allocation 'merely a ceiling' (so Congress can float a range up to 20 percent), yet under the Banat formula 'reaching the ceiling is mandatory' -- 'Isn't this a doctrinal contradiction?'

The Veterans foundation: Veterans Federation Party v. Comelec (2000) translated the four parameters into a formula without striking down any provision (deferring to Congress's discretion and 'limited materials at hand'), acknowledged 'unavoidable distortions' reflecting the law's own, and proposed that 'Congress... revise the law' -- a formula 'unanimously reiterated' in Partido ng Manggagawa (2006) and CIBAC (2007)

The real culprit?: since 'the piece-meal legislation of additional districts' had created 220 districts, CJP asks whether 'what was unconstitutional was the reckless creation of the excessive districts, not the second clause,' and laments that even the ponentes of the recent Veterans-affirming cases concurred in Banat 'with nary a mention' of their own ponencias -- 'So much for doctrinal stability and depth of conviction!'

More problems and the fix: by inflating party-list seats the Court arguably breached the Constitution's cap of 'not more than two hundred and fifty members, unless otherwise fixed by law' -- did it 'usurp the law-making function of Congress'? -- and left open what becomes of the new solons' salaries, pork and three-fourths Charter-change votes if Congress does not pass an enabling law; so 'Congress should take the initiative in correcting the deficiencies,' since 'only Congress has the constitutional mandate to formulate policy solutions' -- 'It is not too late'

one_paragraph_summary: Chapter 6 of 'With Due Respect' (Vol. 5), CJP's April 26, 2009 Inquirer column, sharply critiques Banat v. Comelec, which raised party-list seats 'from 22 to 55' and enlarged the House toward 271. The Court upheld the 'first clause' of Section 1(b) of RA 7941 (an initial seat for a party-list with 'at least two percent of the total votes cast') but struck down the 'second clause' (proportional additional seats) as unconstitutional for making it 'mathematically impossible to achieve the maximum number of available party-list seats when the number... exceeds 50.' To fill the seats, the Court awarded slots to parties with under 2 percent while still capping topnotchers at three -- so Buhay Party's 7.33 percent got only three seats and Cocofed's 0.98 percent got one, and 'a party that gets only 1,000 votes can win. Preposterous, but certainly possible!' If filling 55 seats 'was its passion,' CJP argues, the Court should have struck down both the three-seat limit and the 2-percent threshold entirely (as Justice Nachura urged) to compute with 'legal, mathematical, and proportional precision.' He flags a 'doctrinal contradiction': the Court called the 20-percent allocation 'merely a ceiling' yet made reaching it mandatory, and it 'quietly overlooked' its own recent decisions unanimously reaffirming the Veterans formula -- even those ponentes concurring in Banat 'with nary a mention' ('So much for doctrinal stability and depth of conviction!'). He suggests the true defect may be 'the reckless creation of the excessive districts' (220 of them), not the 'second clause,' and warns that inflating party-list seats past the constitutional cap of 'not more than two hundred and fifty members' may have 'usurp[ed] the law-making function of Congress,' leaving unanswered what becomes of the new solons' salaries, pork and three-fourths Charter-change votes. The fix, he concludes, belongs to the legislature: 'only Congress has the constitutional mandate to formulate policy solutions... It is not too late.'
